analysis.one_liner: Bars leasing federal land that has little or no oil and gas potential, ending speculative leasing.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Energy Committee without a hearing, vote, or any cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop the government from putting federal land up for oil and gas leases when its own analysis shows the land has little or no chance of producing oil or gas. Companies often snap up these cheap leases at minimum bid for speculation, which ties up land used for recreation, grazing, and wildlife while bringing taxpayers almost nothing. The bill would require current assessments of each parcel's oil and gas potential before leasing, with narrow exceptions for land next to producing wells.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently get minimal revenue from speculative leases on low-potential land; people who use public lands for recreation, grazing, hunting, and other uses that existing leases can block; and the agencies that would stop spending resources administering leases that never produce.

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that low- or no-potential federal land is frequently leased at or near the minimum bid or noncompetitively and rarely produces oil or gas, so taxpayers receive minimal revenue from it [S3].
The bill says leases on low- and no-potential land limit the ability of land managers to support other uses like recreation, grazing, timber, and wildlife habitat [S3].

The bill would require the Interior Department to assess and publish the oil and gas development potential of every parcel before offering it for lease, and to bar leasing of parcels designated low or no potential, with exceptions and a variance process [S2].
It would require public notice and at least 60 days of public comment before development assessments and variance decisions are finalized [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that currently acquire cheap speculative leases on federal land with little chance of production, losing a low-cost way to stockpile federal acreage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Speculative federal oil and gas lessees

drawbacks.text: The bill would require updated development assessments before leasing and add a new variance process, which could slow leasing even on land with real oil and gas potential and increase administrative work for the Bureau of Land Management [S3].

Critics of restricting federal leasing generally argue that reduced access to federal acreage can lower domestic production and the federal royalties it generates; the bill itself asserts its policies are not detrimental to US energy security but does not prove that claim [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is modest and well-targeted: it does not ban oil and gas leasing but stops offering parcels the government's own analysis says are unlikely to produce, keeping exceptions for drainage and land near producing wells. The main cost is added process and slower leasing decisions, which is real but limited. The bill leaves the underlying leasing program and its royalty system untouched, so it fixes the most clear-cut waste without addressing broader questions about federal leasing terms.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2020 and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cortez Masto introduced the bill on January 16, 2020 [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without the committee reporting the bill or the Senate voting on it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies holding or seeking cheap speculative leases on low-potential federal land are better off; the current system of minimum-bid leasing on land unlikely to produce remains in place, and taxpayers and public-lands users get none of the bill's benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Speculative federal oil and gas lessees

for.name: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto
for.role: U.S. Senator from Nevada, sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through introduction and referral; no other senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two years it had jurisdiction.

against.name: Sen. Lisa Murkowski
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no other senator cosponsored the bill, so there is no record of where either party stood beyond a single Democratic sponsor.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies leasing federal land
industries.note: The bill would end their ability to acquire cheap, often minimum-bid or noncompetitive leases on federal land its own assessments show has little or no production potential. Those leases tie up public land for other uses while generating minimal revenue for taxpayers, so the industry's interest here runs against the public's.
Ending nonproductive speculative leases would stop agencies from administering leases that yield almost no revenue and free land for grazing, recreation, and habitat.
